facts.statement: Richard Owen formally described the upland moa in 1883.
facts.quote: Richard Owen described the species in 1883.

facts.statement: Richard Owen named the species Dinornis didinus in 1883 based on mummified remains discovered in 1878 by H. L. Squires in Queenstown, New Zealand.
facts.quote: The upland moa was named as Dinornis didinus in 1883 by Richard Owen from mummified material found in 1878 by H. L. Squires in Queenstown, New Zealand and subsequently sent to the British Museum.

facts.statement: The upland moa belongs to the ratites, a group of flightless birds defined by a sternum that lacks a keel.
facts.quote: It belongs to the ratites, a group of predominantly flightless birds characterized by a sternum lacking a keel.

facts.statement: Standing less than one meter tall and weighing between 17 and 34 kilograms, the upland moa is one of the smallest known moa species.
facts.quote: At less than 1 metre tall and about 17 to 34 kilogram in weight, the upland moa is among the smallest known moa species.

facts.statement: Unlike other moas, the upland moa had feathers covering its entire body except for the beak and the soles of its feet, an adaptation for cold environments.
facts.quote: Unlike other moas, it had feathers covering all of its body but the beak and the soles of its feet, an adaptation to living in cold environments.

facts.statement: The upland moa lacked wings and a tail.
facts.quote: The upland moa had no wings or tail.

facts.statement: The upland moa inhabited the South Island of New Zealand, primarily favoring alpine and subalpine environments.
facts.quote: The upland moa inhabited the South Island, where it primarily favored alpine and subalpine environments.

facts.statement: The upland moa traveled to elevations as high as 2,000 meters (7,000 feet) above sea level.
facts.quote: They travelled to elevations as high as 2000 m (7000 ft) above sea level.

facts.statement: Analysis of coprolites suggests the upland moa ate branchlets of trees like Nothofagus, lake-edge herbs, tussock, and nectar-rich flowers.
facts.quote: Studies of the upland moa's coprolites have provided evidence that branchlets of trees such as Nothofagus, various lake-edge herbs, tussock, and nectar-rich flowers made up part of its diet.

facts.statement: The upland moa typically laid only one or two blue-green eggs at a time, likely making it the only moa species to lay non-white eggs.
facts.quote: This moa usually laid only 1 to 2 blue-green coloured eggs at once, and was likely the only type of moa to lay eggs that were not white in colour.

facts.statement: Similar to emus and ostriches, male upland moas cared for their young.
facts.quote: Like the emu and ostrich, male moa cared for the young.

facts.statement: Before humans arrived in New Zealand, the upland moa's only predator was Haast's eagle.
facts.quote: The upland moa's only predator before the arrival of humans in New Zealand was Haast's eagle (Hieraaetus moorei).

facts.statement: The upland moa became extinct around 1500 CE following hunting by the Māori.
facts.quote: Following the arrival of the Māori, the species was hunted and became extinct around 1500 CE.

facts.statement: A 2005 genetic study suggested that Megalapteryx benhami might be a valid species rather than a junior synonym of M. didinus.
facts.quote: In 2005, a genetic study suggested that Megalapteryx benhami, which had previously been considered a junior synonym of M. didinus, may be a valid species after all.

facts.statement: The upland moa belongs to the parent group Megalapterygidae.
The upland moa is classified in the family Megalapterygidae.
The genus Megalapteryx existed from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Gelasian to Holocene (2.58 to 0 million years ago)

rejected.quote: Scientists previously believed that the upland moa held its neck and head upright; however, more recent study has shown that it actually carried itself in a stooped posture, with its head level to its back.
